latently infected T cells in vivo appear phenotypically similar to uninfected cells, that following stimulation, HIV completes its life cycle, and that this process is not accompanied by the induction of a phenotypic marker of cellular activation.
latently infected T cells appear phenotypic normal, but following activation, they express virus and downregulate cell surface markers.

the cell surface phenotype of a latently infected cell is not different from that of a noninfected cell and that HIV expression following activation of the cell does not correlate with expression on the surface of the cell of the activation marker CD25.

HIV infection of T cells is not a static process, but a dynamic one that changes with the activation status of the cell.

latently infected T cells are phenotypically normal, and HIV expression in these cells is not associated with expression of the activation marker CD25, but is associated with phenotypic changes in the infected cell.

The main takeaway from our work is that
latently infected T cells are phenotypically normal and that viral activation does not induce a phenotype that would be easily detected.
the phenotype of the latently infected cells is indistinguishable from that of the noninfected cells, which is a major reason for the difficulty in eradicating the virus from patients.
